extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of fiction; novelists studying description, rhetoric, and performance
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and implicit guidance for producing vivid descriptive prose and dramatic/ornamental passages in fiction — focusing on physical description, oratorical delivery, intonation, emotional authenticity, illustration, and the use of drama to engage readers. Drawn from an illustrative novel passage that mixes stage direction, sermon rhetoric, and authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical posture and stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed physical stance for persuasive public speaking: body swayed and bent forwards at 'an angle of 85 degrees and a half'; right leg sustaining seven-eighths of weight; left foot advanced in a line betwixt them; knee bent 'within the limits of the line of beauty'; right arm falling negligently with the palm open and turned towards the audience; sermon held loosely in the left hand, raised above the stomach and detached from the breast; eyes and facial muscles in harmony; look frank, unconstrained, 'something assured, but not bordering upon assurance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as prescriptive and mechanically explained (weight distribution, 'line of beauty'). Explicitly recommended to painters and 'to orators!' with warning ('unless they practise it,——they must fall upon their noses.'). Example: a statuary might have modelled from the figure. Use these precise physical details to convey authority and persuasive presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise physical/geometrical detail to enhance realism
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of this precise angle of 85 degrees and a half ... shew[s] how the arts and sciences mutually befriend each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that exact, even quasi-technical measurements and geometrical specifics (angles, weight fractions) can strengthen descriptive realism and persuasive effect. Encourages blending exactitude (science) with art to make depiction more convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold and gesture of text-in-hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold the sermon loosely, not carelessly, in the left hand, raised something above the stomach, and detached a little from the breast; right arm falling negligently but palm open and turned towards his audience, ready to aid the sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical handling of a text is part of delivery: neither tight nor careless; placement affects perceived sincerity and readiness to 'aid the sentiment.' Use hand placement/gesture as a signalling device in stage directions or character description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper accent or sneering intonation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'you give that sentence a very improper accent; for you curl up your nose, man, and read it with such a sneering tone, as if the Parson was going to abuse the Apostle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of reading/delivery: intonation must match content and speaker; avoid a sneer or misapplied emphasis that changes sense or alienates listeners. In writing, indicate (or avoid) delivery that contradicts intended sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity improves performance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That was the very reason, _Trim_, replied my father, which has made thee read the sermon as well as thou hast done; ... my heart was so full.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic feeling from the speaker/reader enhances the effectiveness of a delivered text. As a production principle: encourage characters to be genuinely moved (and show it) rather than performatively affectless; authentic engagement translates into more compelling delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spare unnecessary comments while reading
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If he had spared his comments, replied Dr. _Slop_,——he would have read it much better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: excessive explanatory or parental comments during delivery (or intrusive authorial glosses) can weaken the primary performance/reading. Keep interventions minimal to preserve flow and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic (dramatised) writing catches attention
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I like the sermon well, replied my father,—’tis dramatick,—and there is something in that way of writing, when skilfully managed, which catches the attention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice that dramatisation — using theatrical techniques, vivid scenes and emotional peaks — is an effective way to seize reader/listener attention. Caveat: must be 'skilfully managed' (avoid excess melodrama). Example: sermon presented through vivid prison/Inquisition imagery and the reader's emotional reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test the merit of ideas by tracing consequences ('by their fruits ye shall know them')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The surest way to try the merit of any disputed notion is, to trace down the consequences such a notion has produced, and compare them with the spirit of Christianity; ... _By their fruits ye shall know them._'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rhetorical/structural principle for argumentative writing: evaluate ideas by showing their practical outcomes and historical consequences. In fiction, demonstrate beliefs through their fruits (actions, social outcomes) rather than only by abstract assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete illustrative examples and narrative to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermon uses vivid examples (e.g., David and Uriah, the Inquisition, prisons and torture, votaries committing cruelty) to show the consequences of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to prefer concrete anecdotes and descriptive narrative to abstract argument. Vivid, specific instances ('Go with me for a moment into the prisons of the Inquisition') make moral and thematic points more persuasive and emotionally forceful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray moral complexity; avoid simplistic binaries
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As, therefore, we can have no dependence upon morality without religion;—so, on the other hand, there is nothing better to be expected from religion without morality;' and discussion of conscience being unreliable in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thematic rubric: present nuanced, balanced perspectives (show both how religion can support morality and how religion without morality can be dangerous). In storytelling, avoid one-note moralizing; illustrate paradoxes and mixed consequences to enrich thematic depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through precise gesture and small actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Small actions and gestures (wiping tears, bowing, offering a crown to drink with Obadiah, stamping the foot, 'pulling out his handkerchief') are used to reveal character (Trim's honesty, tenderness, simplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minute, concrete gestures and reactions to convey personality and moral tone rather than only explicit labels. Details like how a character handles a handkerchief or reacts to a passage can stand in for exposition and make characters more believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interruptions, asides, and audience reactions to build scene and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene uses multiple interruptions and reactions (father interrupting about accent, Dr. Slop's comments and sleep, uncle Toby's 'Humph!', Trim's exclamations) to shape the pace and comic/serious tone of the reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural technique: intersperse the presented text (e.g., a sermon) with interlocutor reactions, asides, and brief stage directions to create rhythm, reveal relationships, and modulate tension. Anti-pattern: let interruptions be purposeful (character-revealing or pacing) rather than gratuitous.
